words: You mean since I've been married or before?

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Before, anytime, all through your life?

words: Oh yeah, I worked my way through college pretty much. I had help from home, but not too much. I always worked in the summer. I waited tables mostly in the summer . I worked two summers in a logging camp.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Cooking?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: No, just waiting tables. That used to be the big thing in Orofino. I mean, girls , that's what they did, the ones who were really with it, you know. In Orofino, You wouldn't dream of going out and working in someone's house. I mean it was just, yuck. Irma Egland 10

words: It was pretty degrading, then?

words: Yeah. Here, that's what the girls do is go and work for other women; but, we didn't do that in Orofino .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: There's quite a difference in the community of the feeling that way.

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Yeah, I'll say.

words: Was there more money in being a waitress?

words: There was more money in being a waitress, I would say.

words: You'd have certain hours when people would work.

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Oh, yes.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: That's interesting.

speaker: Irma Egland
words: So, I did that , and when I was in school , I had odd jobs at the University. I was a lifeguard for a couple of years . speaker: HE
words: Didn't you work in the bank?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Yeah, I worked in the bank then, too . I stayed out of school a year and worked in the bank in Orofino .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: As a bank clerk?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Oh, teller, I guess . I worked once for six weeks up at Sacred Heart Hospital. I didn't like that , it was in the kitchen just putting stuff on trays . I got terribly bored with that .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Not very stimulating.

speaker: Irma Egland
words: It was okey for a while , but I just as soon look for another job and then, that was when I went back to Orofino and went back to work in the bank. Then, when I came back up to school, I had one more semester. I only had to take about 12 hours, so I had a lot of spare time and I worked half days at First Security Irma Egland 12 Bank in Moscow. Then, after I graduated I went on full time at the bank and worked there for a year .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And that was until you got married, then?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Yes.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And then you quit?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Well, then I went to work in Genesee at the bank and I worked for about six months.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Anything else that you can think of? Kind of a variety of jobs.

speaker: Irma Egland
words: No, I don't think. I went to California one summer and when I went broke, I had to work in a drive-in for a week to get enough money to buy my bus ticket home .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You went out to California by yourself?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: No, I had a very good friend who was from Long Beach and I went down with her.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: This is while you were a student those few years?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Yes. Irma Egland 13

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, you were pretty independent. Tried out quite a few different things.

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Well, yes .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: We asked about other interests, hobbies and talents and some of these are the same up here, like refinishing furniture, the antiques . Is there anything else you can think of?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Oh, I don't know. We have the cattle and I run the hay crew and that type of thing, and do chores a lot.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What do you do when you run a hay crew?

speaker: HE
words: Cook.

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Yeah, cook. Well, you get a bunch of kids out there and they work real good, but they also like to visit. I'm all for visiting, but I think you also have to keep moving a little bit.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You kind of motivate people to get the task done.

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Yeah, they need an adult out there to keep them moving.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: These are local kids you hire?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Well, for years it's been our own, of course, you know, Irma Egland 14 it's family . But we also hire other kids when we get a big rush on. Because we do [unintelligible]. My husband works six, seven days a week and in the summer, he works Sundays at the shop , too . So, it's pretty much up to me, that type of thing .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: How much ranch, farm, do you have here?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: We only have 25 acres here .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So you raise hay.

speaker: Irma Egland
words: We rent about 70 acres and we also, well , he's very busy going out and getting all this hay for us to cut up, and then, of course it's up to the boys and I to do it . Then we sell it. That gives us a little extra.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do you run tractors, things like that?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: No, I won't do that, I just won't do that . I drive truck.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You just oversee and drive the truck?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Well, I used to pitch the bales all the time, but I decided in the last two years that I 'm getting too old. Can't lift them anymore.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: About how heavy are they? Irma Egland 15

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Oh, this year they're awfully heavy, they cut them a little big. They're 60 or 70 pounds.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Those would be above your head.

speaker: Irma Egland
words: It's a hard day's work. If they get wet, they are really heavy. We used to, when the kids and I did most of it, we kept them at 45-50 pounds and I could handle those just fine . These 70 pounders, that's a little heavy for a woman.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And you have cattle that you feed yourself?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: We have a few.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: For beef or for milk?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Oh, they're beef, pretty much. We have one milk cow. It isn't giving milk right now, but we do have one dairy cow, but they're mainly beef.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You spend quite a bit more time taking care of the farm and the family, the home and this are than your husband does. He's usually on the job.

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Oh yes, because he works long hours, so I do it .

words: Do you have any clubs or groups that you are a member of? Irma Egland 16

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Oh, not too much right now. I don't like to belong to anything unless I feel I can take an active part in it. I can see no point in paying dues. Half a dozen different organizations never go anywhere, and so if I can't take an active part then I simply don't belong. Right now I'm on the school board and that keeps me pretty busy. I go to a lot of meetings out of town.

words: Uh huh.

words: Yes .

words: Two years .

words: Is that the term?

words: Will you be running again?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Oh, yes. Irma Egland 17

words: So you must like that.

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Oh, I love it.

words: Are there any other women on the school board?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: No .

words: Oh, no. I think I'm, now, many years ago they said that a lady ran and got on, Mary Cunningham. There used to be two Mary Cunninghams in Genesee and I never did find out which one it was. But she quite soon resigned, I guess . The men really gave her a bad time. I don't know what they did, but at any rate, she soon resigned and I think I've been the first one that has even tried since.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: How do you feel what their attitude is towards you on the board?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Oh, they've been very nice .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do you get a chance to say all you want to and have influence?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Yes . They don' t always care for what I say, but I can say anything I want. Irma Egland 18

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: That doesn't inhibit you from saying it?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: No, they've been very good about it.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do you feel like you've made some changes since you came?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Well, I think, for one thing, I do not really push it but if something comes up on girls' sports and they think, well, there isn't enough interest or something and they ought to cut this out, you know, this part of it, and the girls don't need to do that, well, then I speak up. I say, yes they do, if we offer it for boys, we have to offer it for girls. I think it's made a difference that way. They did try to cut out girls' track this year and I said no . I thought that girls could turn up for, they could use the same coach. They didn't have to have a woman coach for girls' track because that's strictly an individual effort and I thought they could all be under one coach, which I think they're going to do. Other than that, I don't know if I'd made too much of an impact.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Well, it sounds like you speak out and you speak for a group that hasn't been represented in the past.

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Well, I think sometimes, I think the men do a great job of running the school. But I do think women are more interested in the actual children, don't you? Irma Egland 19

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Having been associated with them more where men, I some times think their focus is more on their jobs.

speaker: Irma Egland
words: I think that I have a little different attitude than they do.

words: You certainly have a different viewpoint. I think that's interesting. Have you ever received any awards, honors or ribbons? Were you with Four-H or anything like that?

words: Well, I don't know, not really.

words: It was just where your interest was.

speaker: Irma Egland
words: I belonged to a little neighborhood club around here, oh, it was the C.G. Club, and it's just women out in this area who meet once a month. Irma Egland 20

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, it's just kind of a social get together.

speaker: Irma Egland
words: They do charity work and they take things to the hospital and nursing homes and that type of thing.

speaker: Isabel Miller

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Oh yes. They talk about things that you're interested in.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Okay, that takes care of the personal data sheet. Now, I'll start out on several questions and, like I said before, it's just to stimulate you to go on. Do you see certain advantages in living in rural areas as opposed to living in urban areas?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Oh, yes, and I like the country and the farm life. I think it's a good life; I like a small town. When I was a kid, we lived in the country and we didn't have school buses in those days and, of course, we had to walk and we always thought it would be so neat to live in town. I really envied all my friends; I was the only country girl at that time . But, I always had it in the back of my mind, though, that when I grew up and got married, I was going to live on the farm, too . So, I evidently didn't hate it as much as I thoyght I did.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: It was good for family life?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Oh yes . Yeah, I think it's the only place to live . I don't Irma Egland 21 think I would like it in the city at all .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do you know any women who live in urban areas, personal friends?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: In a large urban area, you mean?

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Yes.

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Well, no, not so much anymore . I used to , but now all my friends are pretty well centered in Genesee.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Can you identify anything to compare to your life to an urban woman's life that would be very different? Can you think of any, certainly, they wouldn't have farm chores like that, of course. The role in her family, for instance, is it different?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: No, I really can't say. I 've never lived in the city, so I just don't know what it would be like. I'm just sure I would not like it. I'm prejudiced.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: As your children were growing up, was it a lot different from what it'd be:en for you when you were growing up at home?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Oh, I don't think so, no .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: When you were growing up at home, did the boys and girls do Irma Egland 22 the same chores, or was there division of work?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Well, at home we did the same thing . Well, there was three girls and just one boy, so , of course, we had to work outside as much as he did. So, I couldn't say, within the family, we weren't treated any differently at all .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So it wasn't really boys' chores and girls' chores; they were supposed to be done and you all did it .

speaker: Irma Egland
words: And my brother could cook. My dad was very good at helping my mother in the house and then she would go out and help him. They worked together . That was kind of the way I was raised. If there was work to be done, we did it and if anyone was going to lay around, everybody laid around.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You got the work done and then everybody could take off. Yes, I understand that . Was it pretty much the same when you were raising your children?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: We've tried to do it that way. Hollis doesn't really care for outside work, but I've needed help in the house, too , because I do work outside and so I needed her in the house . She' s done more cooking and housework than I did when I was growing up .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: This was kind of her preference, was that i t? You'd rather work in the house? Irma Egland 23

speaker: HE
words: Yes .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And you had more brothers that are available for outdoor chores .

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Yes. So that's a difference too. My older sister, the one that lives in Troy, she's a Home Ec teacher. It's just always been that she was an excellent cook, even as a girl , you know, and she still is. She did more of that type of thing.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do the boys help in the house at all?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: My boys? Well, these two younger ones don' t, no, I can't say that they do. The two older ones did, not a great lot, but like on Saturday mornings, they had to clean the basement or something, you know. But, now, these two don't .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: They were just special jobs, special assignments that needed to be done. Did your brothers or sisters go on to college?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: My brother went into the service. He graduated about, it was Pearl Harbor time, so he went into the service for four years .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: He graduated from high school about that time?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Yes. My older sister graduated from the University and my younger sister didn't . After she got out of high school, she Irma Egland 24 just wasn't interested in going on to school . And my folks relaxed a little bit by then, too. Then, when I graduated from high school, I had no interest at all in going on to college. I just didn't want any more school, but I went.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Because your parents expected you to?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Yes, there just was no question about it . I didn't have to go to the University even; in fact, I didn't have to go to college, but I did have to go and learn how to do something. I couldn't just sit around and do nothing, or just get a job. I had to go to secretary school or something. They insisted on that.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Did they see it as kind of a backup for marriage? Did they expect you to get married?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Oh, I imagine they pretty well took it for granted, but they always said that they thought a woman should know how to do something incase she ever had to , you know. I think that's good advice. Everybody should know how to do something.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: They've helped you some, but you've worked quite a bit .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Well, they helped, yeah, quite a bit . They're in cattle ranching and each one of us kids , when we were ten years old, were given a heifer calf. So, then by the time we were in college, Irma Egland 25 we had a pretty good little herd of our own, you see, we had four or five cows. So, then you would have your calves; you'd sell your steer calves and that would give money. So, I would say that was help from the folks because they were our own animals and we were free to do what we wanted; but, it was my parents' land and their hay and dad's work and you know.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Were you supposed to take care of your animals?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Well, we didn't work out too much in the summer in high school because we were expected to be there and help with the haying and we hayed all summer long. That was in the days before the hailers and it was all loose hay and it took quite a while .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And you helped with that?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Yes, and then for the chores , we had lots of cows and some body had to go out every morning and help Dad feed every morning and every night. So we just, when it was your turn, you just went and did it .

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What time did you get up in those days?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Oh, we got up not terribly early. When you read about farm families up at four or five in the morning, none of that . We didn't get up until about six or six-thirty. Irma Egland 26

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So, you had to have your work done before you got to the school bus?

speaker: Irma Egland
words: We didn't have a school bus; we walked . It was two miles and we walked. So, we had to leave early and so we got up and got the chores done first.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: There must have been some pretty cold days.

speaker: Irma Egland
words: Yes, although it isn't as cold in Orofino as it is here. I can remember, though, sometimes there'd be a lot of snow where we lived.
